questions.prompt: Complete: "If it rains tomorrow, we ___ at home."
questions.explanation: The main clause gives the result with will + base verb: we will stay at home. "stayed" is the simple past; "will stays" and "will to stay" change the verb after will, which must stay bare.

questions.prompt: In "If the train goes faster, I'll be on time", what does "I'll be" mean?
questions.explanation: "I'll be" is the short form of "I will be": the future with will in the main clause, the result. It is not "I am" (present), "I was" (past) or "I have been" (present perfect).

questions.prompt: Which clause states the RESULT in "Grandma will make a cake if we visit her on Sunday"?

options.text: if we visit her on Sunday

questions.explanation: The result is the main clause, "Grandma will make a cake" — it has will and it does not start with if. "if we visit her on Sunday" is the condition, even though it comes second; "on Sunday" is only a time, and "if we visit her" is part of the condition.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that follows the comma rule of this chapter:

options.text: You'll feel better, if you drink some water.
If you drink some water you'll, feel better.
If you drink some water, you'll feel better.
If, you drink some water you'll feel better.

questions.explanation: "If you drink some water, you'll feel better." — the if clause comes first, so a comma closes it. When the main clause comes first (You'll feel better if…) there is no comma; the comma never goes inside the result or straight after "If".

questions.prompt: Complete: "If the museum ___ (not open) on Monday, we ___ (visit) it on Tuesday."
questions.explanation: "doesn't open ... will visit": the museum is it, so the if clause takes doesn't + base verb, and the result takes will + base verb. "won't open ... visit" swaps the tenses; "don't" is not for it; "doesn't opens" adds a second -s.

questions.prompt: Karim says: "If I win the race, I will get a medal." Which is TRUE?

options.text: He may win; the medal depends on it.
Karim has already won the race.
Karim will get a medal even if he loses.
Getting a medal is the condition for winning.

questions.explanation: He may win; the medal depends on it: the first conditional talks about a real possibility (winning) and its result (the medal). The race has not happened yet, the medal is not promised if he loses, and the condition is the clause with if — winning, not the medal.
